bugs.summary: abbreviate() can give unexpected output with non-ASCII input
bugs.creator: kevinushey

comments.text:
Created attachment 3681
Use iswlower() rather than islower() when determining if a wide character is lowercase in the current locale.

This is perhaps expected given the warning, but given that this is an issue that could be resolved, here's an example:

```
> abbreviate("přístřešek")
přístřešek
    "přřš"
Warning message:
In abbreviate("přístřešek") : abbreviate used with non-ASCII chars

> R.version
               _
platform       aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
arch           aarch64
os             linux-gnu
system         aarch64, linux-gnu
status         Under development (unstable)
major          4
minor          7.0
year           2026
month          04
day            23
svn rev        89955
language       R
version.string R Under development (unstable) (2026-04-23 r89955)
nickname       Unsuffered Consequences
```

Compare with a similar build of R on macOS, and note the difference in behavior -- likely owing to different behavior in `islower()` between the two different libc implementations.

```
> abbreviate("přístřešek")
Warning in abbreviate("přístřešek") :
  abbreviate used with non-ASCII chars
přístřešek
    "přst"
>
> R.version
               _
platform       aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0
arch           aarch64
os             darwin25.4.0
system         aarch64, darwin25.4.0
status         Under development (unstable)
major          4
minor          7.0
year           2026
month          04
day            23
svn rev        89955
language       R
version.string R Under development (unstable) (2026-04-23 r89955)
nickname       Unsuffered Consequences
```

This comes down to the use of `islower()` rather than `iswlower()` in `wstripchars`. A simple patch is attached.

comments.text:
Created attachment 3682
Use iswlower() rather than islower() when determining if a wide character is lowercase in the current locale. (proper SVN patch)

(In reply to Kevin Ushey from comment #1)
> Created attachment 3682
> Use iswlower() rather than islower() when determining if a wide character is
> lowercase in the current locale. (proper SVN patch)

Thank you, Kevin.

Note that  `help(abbreviate)`  does warn about  using it with non-ASCII characters.  I had hoped that that warning may no longer be necessary, but it **is**:

The result in this case *depends* on the locale (see below)!
On my platform (Fedora Linux 42,43, or 44),
setting the locale, i.e., the here-relevant `LC_CTYPE`, does work,
and the following code --- my proposed regression test, using your example ---
is revealing:
```
ch1 <- intToUtf8(c(112L, 345L, 237L, 115:116, 345L, 101L, 353L, 101L, 107L))
Sys.getlocale() # just for info ..
for(loc in c("C", "C.UTF-8")) {
    lc <- Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", loc)
    if(!is.null(lc) && nzchar(lc)) { # when Sys.setlocale() worked supposedly
        suppressWarnings(a1 <- abbreviate(ch1)) # FIXME - should it warn even when "correct"?
        ## In abbreviate("přístřešek") : abbreviate used with non-ASCII chars
        print(a1) # correctly "přst" *in* case
        print(hasUTF8 <- grepl("utf-?8$", print(Sys.getlocale("LC_CTYPE")), ignore.case=TRUE))
        stopifnot(identical(ch1, names(a1)),
                  identical(c(112L, 345L, if(hasUTF8) 115:116 else c(345L, 353L)),
                            print(utf8ToInt(a1))))
    }
}

```
with the following output (which does *not* render properly in bugzilla/markdown ...):
```
> Sys.getlocale() # just for info ..
[1] "LC_CTYPE=C.UTF-8;LC_NUMERIC=C;LC_TIME=en_US.UTF-8;LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8;LC_MONETARY=en_US.UTF-8;LC_MESSAGES=de_CH.UTF-8;LC_PAPER=de_CH.UTF-8;LC_NAME=C;LC_ADDRESS=C;LC_TELEPHONE=C;LC_MEASUREMENT=de_CH.UTF-8;LC_IDENTIFICATION=C"
```
and the interesting one:
```
p<U+0159><U+00ED>st<U+0159>e<U+0161>ek 
   "p<U+0159><U+0159><U+0161>" 
[1] "C"
[1] FALSE
[1] 112 345 345 353
přístřešek 
    "přst" 
[1] "C.UTF-8"
[1] TRUE
[1] 112 345 115 116
```

Can you try the above R code on your two platforms -- after applying the patch(!!) --
please ?

The exact rendering of the output is of course not the point, but rather that the assertions
are fulfilled for both locale settings...

(I note the encoding of the characters are mangled in the preview in Bugzilla; hopefully they survive the actual post...)


The test for me fails with this patch applied on macOS, even though it succeeded on Linux.

```
> R.version
               _
platform       aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0
arch           aarch64
os             darwin25.4.0
system         aarch64, darwin25.4.0
status         Under development (unstable)
major          4
minor          7.0
year           2026
month          04
day            27
svn rev        89967
language       R
version.string R Under development (unstable) (2026-04-27 r89967)
nickname       Unsuffered Consequences
> ch1 <- intToUtf8(c(112L, 345L, 237L, 115:116, 345L, 101L, 353L, 101L, 107L))
> Sys.getlocale() # just for info ..
[1] "en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8"
> for(loc in c("C", "C.UTF-8")) {
+     lc <- Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", loc)
+     if(!is.null(lc) && nzchar(lc)) { # when Sys.setlocale() worked supposedly
+         suppressWarnings(a1 <- abbreviate(ch1)) # FIXME - should it warn even when "correct"?
+         ## In abbreviate("přístřešek") : abbreviate used with non-ASCII chars
+         print(a1) # correctly "přst" *in* case
+         print(hasUTF8 <- grepl("utf-?8$", print(Sys.getlocale("LC_CTYPE")), ignore.case=TRUE))
+         stopifnot(identical(ch1, names(a1)),
+                   identical(c(112L, 345L, if(hasUTF8) 115:116 else c(345L, 353L)),
+                             print(utf8ToInt(a1))))
+     }
+ }
p<U+0159><U+00ED>st<U+0159>e<U+0161>ek
"p<U+0159>st"
[1] "C"
[1] FALSE
[1] 112 345 115 116
Error: identical(c(112L, 345L, if (hasUTF8) 115:116 else c(345L, 353L)),  .... is not TRUE
Execution halted
```

So there seems to be some inconsistent behavior here when working in a C locale -- however, the test in the UTF-8 locale agrees on both platforms. I'll see if I can learn more.

I think I understand what's happening on macOS. src/main/character.c uses the rlocale.h header, which introduces R's own locale functions when USE_RI18N_FNS is defined. IIUC, this happens in configure.ac:2341-2356, and defaults to on for macOS and Solaris, and off for other platforms.

Notably, this implies that (in "default" builds of R) functions like `iswlower()` are going to be locale-aware on Linux, but not on macOS, where they will behave as though a unicode locale is active regardless of what the current locale actually is.

comments.text:
(In reply to Kevin Ushey from comment #4)

Thank you... the story is even more complicated, somehow.
We can use  `--with-internal-towlower`  to configure R on Linux,
and then it *also* uses R's own locale function.

But contrary to macOS (according to you) it still does not behave "UTF-8 respecting" when in locale `LC_CTIME=C` 

(which I think is correct Linux behaviour but "too helpful" and really wrong behaviour on macOS).

For that reason, I have *not* added any regression test yet when I've committed your patch (+ a NEWS entry) a few minutes ago.
Our regression tests (almost all, notably the  `tests/reg-tests-1*.R` ones)
explicitly set the locale to "C" when running R on the test files, and according to your finding, macOS behaves differently here..

I forget if we can ensure locale  "C.UTF-8" to be available everywhere _and_ settable from R via  `Sys.setlocale()`; if the answer is 'yes' to both, a
regression test using my code (based on your example!) would be fine.

I could close now (bug fixed), .. but am interested in an outcome here.
comments.creator: maechler

comments.text:
> I forget if we can ensure locale "C.UTF-8" to be available everywhere and settable from R via Sys.setlocale(); if the answer is 'yes' to both, a
regression test using my code (based on your example!) would be fine.

Unfortunately, I don't think so. As I understand it, when using glibc on Linux, we can normally only assume the C locale is available, and the desired UTF-8 locales need to be explicitly generated. Typical desktop Linux environments will  provide a UTF-8 locale by default, but others (e.g. minimal server installations) may not come with a UTF-8 locale baked in.

In practice, I think almost all R installations are going to be in environments with a UTF-8 locale available, but it's not a guarantee.

-----

I suppose a related question to all of this is what R _should_ do in these scenarios; e.g. what is the right behavior when working with UTF-8 strings in a C locale?

My bias would be towards being locale-independent in this scenario; e.g. once we have a UTF-8 string, we should be able to classify it the same way regardless of the current locale, but this is quite a larger change and I imagine is contentious. In this world, we could build R to use R's own R18n wrappers on all platforms by default, but is a much larger change.

Sorry, when I initially filed this, I did not think it would prompt such deep questions!
